\section{Bureau Visibility and Affordability Screening}
\label{sec:scenarios}

% Every number is read from thesis/chapters/generated/tab_scenarios.tex (results/raw/rq3s.parquet,
% 100 replicates per arm), tab_cooloff.tex or tab_cap.tex, or from
% results/summary/results_numbers.json, all generated by notebooks/scripts/build_results_tables.py.

This section answers RQ3. The benchmark is the position before the reporting arrangements.
Under bureau visibility, \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the traditional lender's
Regulation 23A test, which is how we model the reported bureau arrangements
\citep{businessday_bnpl_2026}. Under mandatory screening, the same test is applied to every
\ac{BNPL} request, a stricter version of the \ac{FCA}'s affordability check
\citep{fca_ps26_1,woolard2021}. A third arm combines both (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}). Each
arm runs at $\beta=0$ and $\beta=0.3$ with one hundred replicates on shared seeds, so a
difference of 0.13 points in default is detected about half the time and one of 0.2 points
usually.
% switch_se_max = 0.00065 in results_numbers.json; 2 x 0.065 = 0.13.

The two switches move default in opposite directions (Table~\ref{tab:scenarios};
Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios}). Bureau visibility raises it by $0.20 \pm 0.07$ points at $\beta=0$;
at $\beta=0.3$ the rise, $0.10 \pm 0.06$, is not detectable. Screening lowers it by
$0.93 \pm 0.06$ points at $\beta=0$ and $1.03 \pm 0.06$ at $\beta=0.3$. The table's 90+ row is a
share of credit-active households and, as in Section~\ref{sec:results-injection}, is not used
for effects.

Bureau visibility works through refusals. Once the lender sees \ac{BNPL} instalments, it
refuses about 13\% more applications and lends 12 to 15\% less. What it sees is mostly live
instalments: arrears and late fees are 9.9\% of the visible obligation at application, and a
quarter of it is on agreements opened in the same tick against the same shortfall, which a bureau
reporting with a lag would not show.
% arrears_share_at_application (0.099) and live_opened_same_tick_share_at_application (0.25) for
% beta0.all in results/summary/bureau_visible_split.json (notebooks/scripts/check_bureau_visible_split.py,
% seeds 80,000-80,019). 13%: +124/954 and +121/954; 12 to 15%: lever_bureau_beta{0,0.3}_lending_diff
% over lever_bench_beta{0,0.3}_lending (-0.119, -0.150).
A refused household in the model has no other source of credit, so the debt service it cannot
meet becomes arrears. Default rises detectably in Q1 and Q3 at $\beta=0$, by $0.17 \pm 0.08$ and
$0.43 \pm 0.13$ points, and in no quintile at $\beta=0.3$. \ac{BNPL} volume falls by about 1\%,
because the switch acts on traditional lending and not on \ac{BNPL} requests.

The model's rules may favour this result. A refusal can put a household into arrears at once,
whereas a granted loan is repaid over 25 months, partly after the run ends, and the lender
assesses surveyed rather than current income. The switches were not run under the other rules
of Table~\ref{tab:effect} or over a longer horizon, so the result gives the direction of the
affordability channel and is not a forecast.

Screening works on the households that carry the \ac{BNPL} effect. Almost all of its fall in
default is in Q1, $-4.68 \pm 0.10$ points at $\beta=0$ and $-4.70 \pm 0.10$ at $\beta=0.3$, against
a \ac{BNPL} effect in Q1 of about four points (Section~\ref{sec:results-distribution}). The test
refuses \ac{BNPL} to households whose income leaves no room for another instalment, and a refused
shortfall request passes in full to the traditional lender (Algorithm~\ref{alg:gate}), which
applies the same test. Its refusals rise by 1{,}827, close to their level without \ac{BNPL}
(Table~\ref{tab:baseline-arms}). Screening lowers \ac{BNPL} holding by 0.3 points at $\beta=0$
and 0.7 at $\beta=0.3$, and volume by about 3\%, so it removes the effect while leaving most
\ac{BNPL} use in place. Default under screening, 20.88\% at $\beta=0$, is close to the 20.73\% of
the baseline without \ac{BNPL} on other seeds.
% lever_afford_beta0_default (results_numbers.json); baseline_default (seeds 10,000-10,019).

With both switches, default is $0.90 \pm 0.05$ points below the benchmark at $\beta=0$ and
$0.85 \pm 0.05$ at $\beta=0.3$. Against visibility alone, adding screening lowers default by
$1.09 \pm 0.07$ points at $\beta=0$. Against screening alone, adding visibility changes it by
$+0.04 \pm 0.05$ points at $\beta=0$ and raises it by $0.18 \pm 0.06$ at $\beta=0.3$. Peer
influence does not detectably change the benchmark or the effect of either switch
($-0.09 \pm 0.08$ points for bureau visibility).
% switch_both_less_bureau_beta0, switch_both_less_afford_beta{0,0.3}, switch_bench_beta_gap and
% switch_bureau_interaction (+ _se), results/summary/results_numbers.json.

Two further levers, a cooling-off window of one to four ticks after a want-driven purchase and
a hypothetical cap on platforms owed, are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:levers}. None of their
fourteen contrasts with the benchmark is detectable, although the window removes up to 41\% of
\ac{BNPL} volume at $\beta=0.3$ and a cap of one platform removes 35 to 40\%. The window does not
act on borrowing for a shortfall, which is where the \ac{BNPL} effect arises.

\subsection{Answer to RQ3}
\label{sec:scenarios-answer}

Making \ac{BNPL} instalments visible to the traditional lender raises its
refusals by about 13\% and default by $0.20 \pm 0.07$ points without peer influence, because in
the model refused households have nowhere else to borrow; with peer influence the rise is not
detectable. Mandatory screening lowers default by 0.93 to 1.03 points, almost all in the poorest
quintile, about as much as \ac{BNPL} adds. Added to visibility, it removes visibility's rise as
well.
